statements.quote: By placing more behavior into the “default yes” bucket, people with bipolar will do better than those with a default of “no.”
statements.context: Author's maxim for people with bipolar disorder: answer 'yes, until proven otherwise' when asked if one might be manic. Claims that defaulting to yes leads to better outcomes than defaulting to no. Generic habitual claim, not dated.
statements.note: Borderline. Habitual 'will' about a standing pattern, not a dated future state. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: A condition I would deal with for the rest of my life.
statements.context: The author's 2015 streptococcal infection triggered psoriasis, which turned out to be psoriatic arthritis. He states this is a chronic condition he will have for life.
statements.horizon_text: for the rest of my life
statements.note: Borderline personal statement about the author's own chronic illness, not a claim about the world.

statements.quote: But writing something novel, compelling, interesting, concise, funny, or all of those things is not automatic. Not yet. Maybe someday.
statements.context: On ChatGPT: it can write anything on demand but 'it will suck'; good writing is not yet automatic but may become so someday. Hedged call about future AI writing ability.
statements.note: Hedged, undated call about AI writing quality.

statements.quote: Out of respect, you're not gonna get to read any of them yet.
statements.context: The author says he spent the day editing pieces that are not good enough and will hold them back from readers until they are. Statement about this newsletter's own near-term publishing.
statements.note: Trivial statement about the author's own newsletter; later coder likely marks CONTROL.

statements.quote: The public health emergency ends by presidential decree on May 11.
statements.context: Setup of the post: the COVID-19 public health emergency (PHE) ends on May 11, 2023 (post dated May 1, 2023). Dated future event stated as fact; the end of the PHE is what would revert telehealth prescribing rules for controlled substances.
statements.note: Scheduled event stated as fact ten days before it occurs.

statements.quote: Absent any other action, everything at that time will revert to the prior state of the world.
statements.context: Conditional: if the DEA takes no other action before the PHE ends on May 11, 2023, controlled-substance telehealth prescribing rules revert to the pre-pandemic state (Ryan Haight Act in-person requirement). The author goes on to say this is not likely to happen.
statements.note: Conditional; the author immediately says the condition (no action) is unlikely to be met.

statements.quote: That means the Ryan Haight Act will* return! ... *The Above Is Not Likely to Happen.
statements.context: The author states the Ryan Haight Act in-person visit requirement returns when the PHE ends, then footnotes with an asterisk that this is not likely to happen, because the DEA still must read almost 30k public comments on its proposed telemedicine rule. Author's stance: the in-person requirement is unlikely to return on May 11, 2023.
statements.note: Negative call; the asterisk footnote reverses the headline sentence. Quote joins the sentence and its footnote.

statements.quote: Notably, the likelihood that in-office visits will immediately return for everybody everywhere is low. ... I am confident about that statement because I understand that somebody would probably lose their job if that's what happened.
statements.context: Prediction that the DEA will not let the in-person visit requirement for controlled-substance prescribing snap back for all telehealth patients when the PHE ends May 11, 2023. Reasoning: organizational self-preservation at the DEA; a snap-back would be a public health disaster with congressional hearings.
statements.confidence_phrase: likelihood ... is low; I am confident
statements.note: Core call of the post.

statements.quote: To let the public health emergency expire with no action from the DEA as it relates to the millions of people who are now getting their controlled substances prescribed via telehealth? That would be a public health disaster; somebody would look like a huge dope, there would be congressional hearings, somebody would get fired, and other people would be embarrassed.
statements.context: Conditional consequence forecast: if the DEA takes no action before the PHE expires, there would be a public health disaster, congressional hearings and firings. Used as the reason the DEA will act.
statements.note: Conditional on DEA inaction; the author expects the condition not to occur.

statements.quote: It's impossible to get everybody who is getting care by telehealth to physical in-person providers who don't exist instantly. It would be a disaster. So it won't happen.
statements.context: Negative call: an instant return to in-person-only prescribing of controlled substances after the PHE ends will not happen.
statements.note: Restates the core call in flat negative form.

statements.quote: The can will be kicked down the road. There will be an extension.
statements.context: Prediction that the DEA will extend the COVID-era telehealth flexibilities for controlled-substance prescribing past the May 11, 2023 PHE end rather than let them lapse.
statements.note: First of three linked calls: extension, probable second extension, eventual resolution.

statements.quote: There will be another extension probably.
statements.context: Second linked call: after a first extension of the telehealth controlled-substance prescribing flexibilities, the DEA will probably extend again.
statements.note: Second of three linked calls.

statements.quote: And eventually, they'll figure it out.
statements.context: Third linked call: the DEA will eventually settle a permanent rule for telehealth prescribing of controlled substances.
statements.note: Third of three linked calls; vague resolution criterion.

statements.quote: Experts will have industry involvement and conflicts of interest in the AI-driven healthcare age.
statements.context: After resigning from an AACAP CME planning committee because of ACCME ineligible-company rules, the author argues that in the coming AI-driven healthcare era experts will routinely have industry ties, which current CME rules cannot accommodate.
statements.note: General forward-looking claim about the profession; not dated.

statements.quote: That resignation comes with a warning: not everyone who has a conflict will do what I just did. 100% of the people looking to scam us will not take that step.
statements.context: Closing warning: others with conflicts of interest will not self-report and resign as the author did; people looking to scam will never take that step.
statements.note: Generic behavioral prediction with a stated 100% figure.

statements.quote: This also means that the party is over. It is time for psychedelic treatments to get boring. Fast.
statements.context: The AMA approved a CPT III code for psychedelic therapies. The author reads this as the end of the festival era: psychedelic medicine will now have to become conventional, 'boring' medicine. Partly exhortation.
statements.note: Borderline: 'the party is over' is declarative but the sentence also reads as advice. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: We will have some sense of what it means in July 2023.
statements.context: Author's restatement of the press release that the AMA is expected to release full details of the psychedelic therapy CPT III code in July 2023.
statements.note: Endorsed restatement of an AMA press-release timeline.

statements.quote: Eventually, we will know what the code is in 2024.
statements.context: Author's restatement of the press release: the psychedelic therapy CPT III code goes into effect when published on January 1, 2024.
statements.note: Endorsed restatement; the quoted source says effective January 1, 2024.

statements.quote: I believe psychedelic medicine has tremendous promise.
statements.context: Author's overall stance on the future value of psychedelic medicine, stated before arguing the field must adopt a sober medical culture to be accepted.
statements.note: Borderline: promise statement without a concrete resolvable claim.

statements.quote: I have it on good authority that experts in the space will be doing so promptly.
statements.context: Footnote: the CPT III codes are experimental and have no relative value units (RVUs), so no payment amount can be derived yet; the author says experts will promptly work on converting them to payment after the review of rules and regulations.
statements.confidence_phrase: I have it on good authority ... will
statements.note: Second-hand but adopted by the author.

statements.quote: Don't Feed the Trolls: Substack's Content Moderation Punt Will Destroy the Platform.

statements.note: Headline claim; restated in the body ('will destroy this company').

statements.quote: an annotated exploration of horrific contact moderation decisions that will destroy this company
statements.context: Body restatement of the title claim, addressed to Substack CEO Chris Best: content moderation decisions will destroy Substack.
statements.note: Restatement of the headline call.

statements.quote: This time, clearly, given the scope of the tragedy, it will be different, and meaningful change is definitely going to happen thanks to the actions of brave lawmakers representing this locality.
statements.context: Sarcastic template text quoted from the author's earlier article on child gun deaths. The sincere reading is the inverse: no meaningful gun-policy change will follow any given shooting.
statements.note: Satire: the literal claim is not the author's expectation; sincere reading is that meaningful gun legislation will not happen.

statements.quote: I regret to inform you the obtuse nerd humor is going to continue unabated.
statements.context: Closing line: the author will keep writing in his satirical style on this newsletter.
statements.note: Trivial statement of intent about the author's own newsletter.

statements.quote: Selling drugs illegally is illegal, and the people doing that can and should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law… until we decriminalize those things as well.
statements.context: Aside in the author's 'keynote' on DEA regulation and diversion, implying he expects eventual decriminalization of currently illegal drug sales.
statements.note: Borderline: 'until we decriminalize' implies an expectation but sits inside a normative sentence.

statements.quote: I wonder if there was some way we could take phenomenal amounts of money plus innovative ideas in healthcare and change anything? Probably not. It's just a crazy dream.
statements.context: Satirical riff on UnitedHealth Group's 'Until It's Fixed' podcast: despite $330 billion in annual revenue, UHG will probably not change anything in healthcare. Satirical framing; the underlying expectation reads as sincere.
statements.note: Satirical framing; underlying claim (UHG will not use its resources to change healthcare) reads as the author's real expectation.

statements.quote: There is no solution to the problem of being the largest healthcare company on earth, there's only the relentless pursuit of getting even bigger.
statements.context: Author's claim about UnitedHealth Group's trajectory: it will keep pursuing growth rather than fix healthcare.
statements.note: Present-tense characterization with a forward-looking reading (continued growth pursuit).

statements.quote: I'm going to make fun of UnitedHealth group, because they have $330 billion in revenue.
statements.context: Statement of intent: the newsletter's satire will continue to target UnitedHealth Group.
statements.note: Trivial intent statement about the author's own newsletter.

statements.quote: Today, it is the One Ring; tomorrow, it could be the Historic Shire.
statements.context: Satirical press release from Mordor Inc. after Optum (UnitedHealth Group) destroys the One Ring following a Series D round led by Optum Ventures. The line jabs at acquirers destroying acquired companies' assets; the literal claim is fiction.
statements.note: Satire/fiction. Logged for recall; underlying jab is that Optum/UHG acquisitions destroy acquired innovations.

statements.quote: We don't yet have the elaborate tools for a psychiatric diagnosis that we imagined on Star Trek. I have been told they are coming.
statements.context: APA dispatch on measurement-based care: elaborate psychiatric diagnostic tools do not exist yet, but the author relays that they are coming; meanwhile validated rating scales are available and should be recorded item by item.
statements.confidence_phrase: I have been told they are coming
statements.note: Relayed from unnamed sources; the author neither endorses nor disputes. Undated.

statements.quote: And that is on the verge of changing…Follow for More!
statements.context: Explainer on how inpatient psychiatric care is paid (per diem or IPF PPS, not DRGs), which left psychiatric hospitals no incentive for efficient discharge and no mechanism to pay for innovative treatments. The author says this is about to change with the 2024 CMS update that inspired the article.
statements.note: Refers to the 2024 CMS IPF PPS update mentioned earlier in the post; foreshadows a follow-up.
